claims.text: Rapid heating followed by rapid cooling can produce a metastable, single-phase high-entropy nanoparticle solid solution by suppressing secondary-phase formation.
A short high-temperature dwell kinetically traps the constituent elements because atomic diffusion is limited.
The kinetically trapped baseline is a homogeneous random solid solution.
The proposed starting material is a uniformly mixed precursor containing more than five noble-metal compounds.
The controlled intervention is to extend dwell time while holding peak temperature and rapid cooling rate constant.
At fixed peak temperature, a longer dwell increases the time available for diffusion and atomic rearrangement.
With sufficient dwell time, atoms rearrange in response to thermodynamic affinities or enthalpic driving forces.
Extending the high-temperature dwell promotes phase separation, elemental segregation, or secondary-phase formation relative to the short-dwell baseline.
Increasing the number of elements can kinetically hinder ordering and segregation because each atom type becomes more dilute and mobility is restricted.
Rapid thermal nanoparticle synthesis can involve heating on a tens-of-milliseconds timescale and cooling rates of at least 10^4 K/s.
The short-dwell synthesis regime is non-equilibrium and too brief for full thermodynamic equilibration.
The applicable peak-temperature range is approximately 1100–2000 K with millisecond dwell times.
The hypothesis may cease to apply if extended dwell causes thermal decomposition or extensive grain growth.
The transition dwell time varies with nanoparticle composition and processing parameters.
X-ray diffraction and spatially resolved microscopy or elemental mapping can test for secondary phases and compositional inhomogeneity.

A controlled null result in which extended-dwell and baseline samples remain statistically indistinguishable in phase homogeneity, segregation, and crystal structure would falsify the proposed dwell-time mechanism.
